title: Passion Identification Questions
opening: Look for what you repeatedly return to. A possible passion is a candidate to examine, not a permanent job identity.

source.manuscript: Passion Identification Questions begins with experience: what absorbs you, returns to mind unprompted, draws you without payment or brings you back through difficulty? Name the compelling feature of each answer and compare patterns across activities.
source.attribution: Supplied recovered manuscript; authorship/adoption of every wording is not independently established.
source.boundary: This inquiry can suggest a candidate; it does not prove a permanent calling. Paid and unpaid experience can both matter. Nonparticipation may reflect access, time, health, obligation or other conditions, so it does not by itself disprove attraction. If a real try repeatedly differs from the imagined appeal, revise the candidate.

example.title: The repeated feature can travel across settings
example.body: Illustrative case: at work, a person helps a new teammate understand unfamiliar software; at home, they make a confusing recipe easier for a sibling; alone on a commute, they sketch a clearer explanation and return to improve it after a rough first draft. The shared draw may be making difficult ideas clear. The person can test that candidate with one short peer explanation; it does not mean every future job must be teaching. Separately, they imagine enjoying indoor climbing but have not tried it because classes cost too much. That is an imagined interest plus an access barrier, not evidence against attraction. A free introductory session could produce the first actual observation.
